intro.title: Tool Introduction
intro.problem1: Software engineers have always faced a contradiction when drawing diagrams: flowcharts and architecture diagrams drawn with tools like Visio and Figma look great, but modification costs are extremely high — half a day spent dragging and aligning, then changing one node requires re-layouting everything. Worse, binary files generated by these tools can't be added to Git version control, leading to team collaboration chaos where "your diagram looks different from what I see." Mermaid solves this contradiction — it defines diagrams using plain text syntax, code IS the diagram, modifying text updates the graphic, naturally supporting diff and version control.
intro.problem2: This tool is a complete Mermaid online workstation: left side features a CodeMirror 6-based code editor (syntax highlighting, auto-wrap, fullscreen), right side has a real-time preview area (auto re-renders 300ms after code changes). Supports 8 diagram types: flowchart, sequence, state, class, ER, pie, Gantt, and user journey. Built-in e-commerce examples — from order flows to user journeys, click to see complex diagram examples.
intro.problem3: All rendering and exporting happens locally in the browser — your system architecture diagrams, database designs, and business processes are never uploaded to any server. Results can be exported as PNG (2x resolution, suitable for document insertion) or SVG (vector lossless, suitable for web embedding and printing). GitHub, GitLab, Notion, Typora, and other platforms natively support Mermaid rendering — diagrams created here can be displayed by simply copying the code into documents.
intro.format1: Mermaid was created by Knut Sveidqvist in 2016, initially just to simplify flowchart drawing. After years of community development, it has become the most popular "diagrams as code" tool — natively supported by GitHub, with dozens of VS Code plugins, and integrated into Notion/Obsidian/Typora and other note-taking tools. Mermaid's design philosophy is "express maximum information with minimum code" — a simple flowchart requires just three lines: flowchart TD, A[Start], A --> B[End]. This tool always tracks the latest stable Mermaid version, ensuring support for all published diagram types and syntax features.
intro.core1: Real-time Preview Engine: Auto re-renders with 300ms debounce after code changes — ensuring immediate feedback while avoiding rendering storms from frequent typing. When syntax errors occur, the preview shows error location and cause (precise to line number), helping quickly locate typos or unclosed brackets. Supports 10 theme color switches, one-click visual style changes.
intro.core2: Interactive Navigation: Large diagrams (50+ nodes) inevitably exceed the screen. Scroll wheel zoom (10%-500%) + mouse drag panning allows free browsing of any diagram area. Fullscreen mode hides all UI elements, keeping only the diagram — ideal for presentations and screenshots.
intro.core3: Dual-format Export: PNG uses Canvas rasterization at 2x resolution (Retina level) by default, suitable for Word/PPT/email insertion. SVG outputs vector files directly, lossless at any magnification, suitable for web embedding, print design, and importing into Figma for further editing.
intro.core4: Data Security: Pure frontend rendering, no network transmission. Architecture diagrams, database designs, and business processes you draw always stay in your local browser, never uploaded or cached on any server. Closing the tab clears everything completely.

instructions.title: User Guide
instructions.chart1: Flowchart — Describe Steps and Decisions: Use nodes for steps, connecting lines for flow, diamonds for decision branches. Node shapes include rectangle [text], rounded rectangle (text), diamond {condition}, parallelogram >input], etc. Connection lines support solid -->, dashed -.->, thick ==>, with optional text labels -->|yes|. Layout direction uses TD (top→down) or LR (left→right). Suitable for approval workflows, algorithm logic, system deployment architecture.
instructions.chart2: Sequence Diagram — Describe Interaction Order: Message passing between multiple participants (people, systems, microservices). Use ->> for synchronous requests, -->> for responses, -x for failures. Combined fragments support loop (循环), alt/else (conditional branches), par (parallel), opt (optional). Suitable for API call chains, login authentication flows, microservice interactions.
instructions.chart3: State Diagram — Describe State Transitions: All states of an object throughout its lifecycle, and events that trigger transitions. Use [*] for start/end states, --> for transitions, with trigger conditions on arrows. Supports composite states (state nesting) and parallel regions. Suitable for order state machines (pending→paid→shipped→completed), device operating states, approval workflows.
instructions.chart4: Class Diagram — Describe Object-Oriented Structure: Each class has three layers: class name, attributes, methods. Relationship types: inheritance <|--, realization ..|>, association --, composition *--, aggregation o--, dependency ..>. Supports multiplicity notation (1:1, 1:N). The standard diagram for expressing system architecture, domain models, and database design.
instructions.chart5: ER Diagram — Describe Database Structure: Entities (tables) contain names and attribute lists (with optional type annotations). Relationships support one-to-one ||--||, one-to-many ||--o{, many-to-many }o--o{. Suitable for showing table structure design and constraints before development; the standard expression for database modeling.
instructions.chart6: Pie Chart — Show Proportional Distribution: Minimalist syntax — "label" : value, values automatically calculate percentages. Suitable for market share, budget allocation, user composition, and other "part-to-whole" relationships. Supports show-data to display specific values.
instructions.chart7: Gantt Chart — Show Project Progress: Group with section, annotate each task with start time and duration days. Status markers: done (completed), active (in progress), crit (critical path), milestone. Suitable for sprint planning, project scheduling, development progress.
instructions.chart8: User Journey — Show Experience Flow: Each step annotates participating roles and experience scores (1-5). Displays the complete path from initial contact to task completion on a timeline, helping identify pain points. Suitable for UX research — registration experience, shopping path analysis, feature usability assessment.

notes.title: Notes
notes.syntax1: Strict case matching is the most common pitfall for beginners. flowchart must not be written as Flowchart, sequenceDiagram must be camelCase, and stateDiagram-v2's -v2 cannot be omitted. Keyword spelling errors cause the entire diagram to fail rendering, and error messages aren't always clear — when encountering rendering issues, check keyword spelling line by line first.
notes.syntax2: Node IDs are the diagram's "variable names" — only English letters, numbers, and underscores are allowed; no spaces or special characters. If node text needs to contain Chinese, spaces, or special symbols, wrap them in double quotes: A["User Login"], B["Step 1: Initialize"]. Node IDs must be unique within a diagram; duplicate IDs are treated as the same node.
notes.syntax3: Bracket closure is the most common syntax error. A[text missing the closing square bracket, or B(text missing the closing parenthesis will crash the entire diagram. Error messages appear in the preview, but sometimes only say "syntax error" without indicating the exact location. It's recommended to check the preview after every 3-5 nodes to avoid accumulating hard-to-locate errors.
notes.syntax4: Chinese characters are fully supported in Mermaid v10+, but certain special punctuation (like Chinese quotes “”, full-width parentheses) may still cause parsing anomalies. It's recommended to use standard Chinese punctuation for node text, and wrap label text on connection lines in double quotes. If Chinese node rendering appears offset, try adding spaces before and after the text.
notes.performance1: Empirical thresholds: 50 nodes for flowcharts, 15 participants for sequence diagrams, 30 tasks for Gantt charts — rendering time may exceed 1 second beyond these values. Large diagrams with over 100 nodes may cause noticeable browser lag. Strategy: use subgraph to group related nodes (subgraph nesting recommended no more than 3 levels deep), or split large diagrams into multiple simpler ones for layered display.
notes.performance2: Real-time preview triggers rendering after each code modification. The tool has a built-in 300ms debounce — rendering executes only after you stop typing, avoiding rendering storms from frequent keypresses. The editor may briefly lag during rendering of large diagrams — this is normal, as Mermaid's layout algorithm needs to calculate positions and connection paths for every node.
notes.performance3: If you only need to understand diagram structure without precise rendering, paste the diagram code into a plain text editor — Mermaid syntax itself has good readability, and you can understand the logic expressed by the diagram even without rendering.
notes.compatibility1: This tool uses Mermaid v10+, supporting all modern browsers (Chrome 80+, Firefox 75+, Edge 80+, Safari 13+). Chrome/Edge recommended for best rendering performance. IE is not supported — Mermaid depends on SVG and ES6 features. Mobile devices can view and share diagrams, but editing large diagrams isn't ideal.
notes.compatibility2: Mermaid code is cross-platform portable — code written in this tool can be directly pasted into GitHub README, GitLab Wiki, Notion, Obsidian, Typora, and other Mermaid-supporting platforms for rendering. If your code doesn't render on other platforms, they may be using an older Mermaid version — this tool always uses the latest stable version.
notes.compatibility3: Exported PNG images display correctly on all platforms and devices. SVG files can be opened directly in browsers, or imported into design tools like Figma and Illustrator for further editing. It's recommended to save both source code and exported images — source code for modifications, images for current display.
notes.export1: PNG export uses Canvas rasterization of SVG, defaulting to 2x resolution (approximately 192 DPI), sharp and clear on Retina screens. Suitable for Word documents, PPT presentations, email, instant messaging. File size depends on diagram complexity — simple diagrams approximately 50-200KB, complex diagrams may exceed 1MB.
notes.export2: SVG is a vector format, lossless at any magnification. File size is typically smaller than PNG (simple diagrams approximately 5-30KB). Suitable for web embedding (can be referenced with <img> tags), print design, and importing into design tools for editing. SVG files are essentially XML text and can be opened and modified with a text editor.
notes.export3: Best practice: store .mmd source files alongside project documentation in your Git repository. Each diagram modification only requires changing a few lines of text, no need to redraw. Export images for current document display, source files for future maintenance. This "code as diagram" approach is much more efficient than maintaining a bunch of .png/.vsdx files.
notes.security1: System architecture diagrams, database ER diagrams, business flow diagrams you draw — all Mermaid code editing and rendering happens entirely locally in the browser. Even if diagrams contain sensitive information like internal system names, API addresses, database table structures, nothing is transmitted over the network to any server. You can verify with F12 developer tools' Network panel.
notes.security2: When using on public devices, be aware: although data isn't uploaded, browsers may cache page content. Before leaving, close all related tabs. This tool doesn't use localStorage to persist edited content; closing the tab immediately clears code and diagrams from memory.
notes.security3: If you need to draw architecture diagrams containing trade secrets, it's recommended to use incognito mode on your personal computer — incognito mode doesn't retain any browsing history, cache, or cookies after closing.
notes.faq1: Diagram renders blank or errors? Check line by line: 1) Keyword spelling and case (flowchart, not Flowchart); 2) All brackets and quotes closed; 3) Node IDs don't contain illegal characters; 4) Connection line syntax correct (--> must not be written as ->). The preview's error message will indicate the approximate location.
notes.faq2: Flowchart nodes overlapping or layout messy? Try: 1) Switch layout direction (TD↔LR); 2) Group related nodes with subgraph; 3) Shorten node text (overly long text causes excessively wide nodes); 4) Reduce node count, split into multiple subgraphs. Layout algorithms differ significantly by direction; sometimes changing direction solves the problem.
notes.faq3: Want to customize theme colors? Add initialization directive at the beginning of your code: %%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#EA580C', 'lineColor': '#333'}}}%%. You can customize primary color, line color, text color, etc. Preview updates immediately after modification. This is more flexible than using preset theme dots.
notes.faq4: Exported PNG is blurry? This may be caused by browser zoom. This tool defaults to 2x resolution rendering. If you need higher resolution (e.g., for large-format printing), it's recommended to download SVG then export at the desired resolution in professional tools, or zoom the diagram in the browser and take a screenshot.
